Studies at the colleges the curriculum consisted of prescribed studies. They were English literature and rhetoric, Latin and, in many of them, Greek, history, some science, mathematics, inductive logic, moral philosophy, and political economy, and often a little psychology and metaphysics. Perhaps some ancient or general history was added. French and German were commonly taught. The students in these colleges rarely were over twenty when they received the degree of bachelor of arts, and then entered on the study of law, medicine, and theology at some professional school, or went into business or into teaching in the secondary schools. This was the almost universal process of American higher education a generation ago.

    The second and third quotations modify the dimensions of the measuring stick to fit collegiate institutions in the South and Southwest. First, Thomas M. Curry as United Commissioner of Education in his annual report was forced to state:

    One of the most discouraging features in our system of higher education has been . . . in a large part of the country, the low standard of scholarship exacted of institutions when they are chartered and authorized to confer degrees. This condition of affairs is largely, if not entirely, responsible for the large number of small, poorly equipped degree-conferring institutions which are no better than high schools.
